_comment: Storyboard for the Grade 3 Science unit lecture film, Lesson 1 Living, Once Alive, Never Alive. Rendered by tools/create-ehel-unit-lecture.js. See lecture-video/BRIEF.md. The five lecture parts in their order (what every living thing does, once alive, never alive, five ways to find out, a question you can test), in the lesson's own words and examples: the four life processes as its explore step names them, each shown in a cat and in a plant as its explain() pairs them; the tree cut down and made into a chair, the sheep's wool, the paper book and the leather shoe of its demo and its sort; the stone, spoon, drinking glass and plastic cup, and the three bins of its sort; the five enquiries with its own example questions; the snails of its ask step. The misconception it corrects is the lesson's own: wood and paper are not never alive, so ask where a thing came from.
title: Living, Once Alive, Never Alive
subtitle: Grade 3 Science
objectives: Describe differences between things that are living, that were once alive and that have never lived.
Know that life processes common to plants and animals include nutrition, growth, movement and reproduction.
Know that there are five main types of scientific enquiry (research, fair testing, observing over time, identifying and classifying, and pattern seeking).
Ask scientific questions that can be investigated.
Use observations and tests to sort, group and classify objects.

beats.say: Look at a cat, a wooden chair and a stone.
The cat is living. The chair was once alive. The stone never was.
Every living thing does four things. We call them life processes.
Nutrition means taking in food. A cat eats. A plant makes its own food from sunlight.

at.plant: A plant makes its own food

beats.say: Growth means getting bigger. A kitten grows into a cat, a seedling into a tree.
Movement means moving by itself. A cat runs. A plant turns its leaves towards the light.
Reproduction means making more of your own kind. Cats have kittens. Plants make seeds.
A cat does all four. So does a tree, only slowly.
Some things are not alive now, but they came from something that was.
A tree is cut down. The wood is no longer alive.
The wood is made into a chair. The chair was once alive.
A woollen jumper was a sheep's coat. A paper book was a tree too.
A leather shoe was once alive too: leather is animal skin.
A stone, a metal spoon, a drinking glass, a plastic cup.
None of these ever ate, grew, moved by itself or had young.
They were never alive. So there are three groups, not two.
To sort a thing, ask where it came from. Wood and paper come from trees.
Scientists find things out in five ways. These are the five types of enquiry.
Research means looking it up. How far away is the Moon?

at.moon: How far away is the Moon?

beats.say: In a fair test, you change one thing. Does more water make a plant grow taller?
Observing over time: watch something change. How does a tadpole change each week?
Identifying and classifying: sort things into groups by what they are like.
Pattern seeking: measure lots of things and find a pattern. Do taller children have bigger feet?
A scientist's question is one you can answer by looking, testing or looking up.
Do snails move faster on wet ground? You can test that.
Time the same snail over the same distance, first on wet ground, then on dry.
Are snails nice? You cannot test that.
So ask: how would I find out? Today, you will ask a question you can test.
Living things take in food, grow, move and make more of their own kind.
Wood, paper, wool and leather were once alive. Rock, metal and glass never were.
Scientists find out in five ways, and ask questions they can test.
